fields.title: Prune duplicate project rows left by a path-resolution bug
fields.description: Prune duplicate project rows whose paths resolve to the same directory, refusing unless the duplicate is provably empty and re-pointing its references instead of orphaning them.
fields.context:
E-2002 stops the Go hook auto-registering a second project for a directory that already has one, and makes lookups tolerate rows stored unresolved — but it deliberately ships no migration, so a ledger that already caught the bug keeps its junk row (typically named <project>-2, path unresolved, zero tasks, bound to whatever sessions ran while the bug was live).

It is inert after E-2002 (lookups prefer the lower id) but still shows up in `endless project list` and in any per-project rollup.
fields.analysis: Consider whether this belongs in `endless project purge` or a doctor-style command.

fields.title: Stop hard-deleting sessions, decisions and projects

fields.context:

fields.title: Store project paths home-relative
fields.description: Store project paths relative to the home directory with a tilde prefix, keeping absolute paths only outside it, while still passing expanded paths to the filesystem and git.
fields.analysis:
Touches from E-2002 that all move together: monitor.NormalizeProjectPath, MatchProjectPath, ProjectPath and RepairProjectPaths; endless.project_path normalize, match_project_path and project_name_for_cwd; the hook's single cwd normalization at entry; the CLAUDE.md rule; tests on both sides and tests-tasks e-2002-verify.sh.

ProjectPath is the risky one — every caller currently treats its return as a real path (worktree roots, lock files, git invocations, the claim handoff cd line). It should keep returning the RESOLVED form; only the stored column and the comparison path change shape.

Sequencing note: E-2009 refuses registering anything outside $HOME, which makes the tilde form near-universal and the mixed-form case rare. Neither task blocks the other, but doing E-2009 first shrinks the surface this one has to prove.

Measured beforehand, so nobody re-derives it: the byte saving is not the reason. projects.path holds 53 home prefixes, about 954 bytes of a 102 MB database. The reason is readability, recorded in ED-1562.

## From the description

A tilde string is not a filesystem path in Go or Python, so the single accessor must split in two — a STORED form (home-relative, used for writes and comparisons) and a RESOLVED form (absolute, used for anything touching disk) — with names that make the difference obvious at the call site. Comparisons happen in stored form; symlinks are still resolved before relativizing. A change file rewrites existing rows, as E-2002's did.

$HOME being unset or wrong must fail loudly, never silently yield a bad path.

fields.title: Fix add-to-lessons pointing at a retired lessons file
fields.description: Fix the add-to-lessons command to record lessons through endless lesson write instead of appending to a retired lessons file in the main checkout.
fields.context:
Both halves contradict Endless's CLAUDE.md: the file lives at .endless/LESSONS.md relative to the worktree root (.claude/ is the harness's directory; this is an Endless artifact), and E-2000 explicitly forbids appending to the main checkout's copy from a worktree — it is tracked, so it strands an uncommitted change in a checkout belonging to no branch and no task, the isolation break worktrees exist to prevent. The retired ~/.claude/LESSONS.md also still exists, so a session that obeys the command writes a lesson nobody reads. Discovered during E-2005: the command was invoked, contradicted CLAUDE.md, and CLAUDE.md was followed instead.

The command file has a .bak dated 2026-08-20 03:17, so it was edited today and may simply predate the move.

fields.title: Fix land failing to record a landing after a symbol rename
fields.description: Fix worktree land so recording the landing still works when the branch renames a Python symbol, which breaks today because land merges new source under its own running process.
fields.context:
`endless worktree land` runs from the main checkout's editable install and ff-merges main underneath its own live process, so modules imported AFTER the merge come from the new source while ones already in sys.modules stay at the old one.

E-2011 renamed endless.project_path.normalize to resolved, main advanced, and recording the landing died on `cannot import name 'resolved' from 'endless.project_path'` — leaving no task_landings row and the branch tip unmerged.

Re-running lands cleanly because a fresh process loads the new source throughout, so this is a half-completed land and a confusing error, not corruption.
fields.analysis:
Candidate fixes: re-exec the CLI immediately after the Step 5 ff-merge so all post-merge work runs on the new source; or run the record step as a subprocess. Either way the invariant to establish is that no post-merge code path shares a process with pre-merge imports.

Note the failure is order-dependent and so will not reproduce reliably: it fires only when the renamed symbol is referenced by a module that had NOT yet been imported when the merge happened. On E-2011 that module was endless.event_bridge, reached through the landing-record emit.

## From the description

self_dev-only (a downstream land does not replace endless's own code), but every self_dev land of a Python rename is exposed.

fields.description: Enforce the documented status lifecycle in task update, refusing status changes that are not edges in it and work-progress statuses set by a session that does not hold the task.
fields.notes: Natural home is E-1891's status registry.
fields.context:
`task update --status` accepts any status from any status, from any actor, regardless of whether a session ever claimed the task.

Observed 2026-08-20: a session holding E-1817 ran `endless task update E-2015 --status unverified` on a task that was `unplanned`, had never been claimed, had no worktree and no session — so `session goto E-2015` found nothing to go to.

The lifecycle is byte-synced across three docs by a test while nothing checks the lifecycle itself.
fields.analysis:
## Should docs/status-lifecycle.mmd be the source for the guard? (Mike, 2026-08-20)

Yes — but not as a runtime dependency, and not against the diagram as it stands
today.

### The parse is genuinely deterministic

`stateDiagram-v2`'s transition syntax is a tiny regular subset: `A --> B: label`.
One regex over the file extracted every edge cleanly on the first try. No LLM,
no ambiguity, no `claude -p`.

### The diagram today is NOT complete enough to derive from

Measured, not assumed — parsing the current file gives:

- **`blocked` does not appear at all.** It is a status in the guide's table but
  has no node and no edges. A diagram-derived table would refuse every
  transition into or out of `blocked`.
- **`completed` has no inbound edge.** Only `completed --> revisit` and
  `completed --> [*]`. Nothing draws how a task REACHES `completed` — yet
  research tasks land there (ED-1502), and E-1817 itself is `completed`. A
  diagram-derived guard would have refused the exact transition that closed the
  task that filed this one.

Both are documentation defects that have been invisible because nothing consumed
the diagram. That is the argument FOR doing this: deriving from it converts them
into a failing test on day one.

### The diagram cannot express two axes the guard needs

- **Actor.** Edge labels carry it as prose — "user approves", "session claims",
  "agent submits", "triage routes". Consistent enough to become a label grammar,
  but that would make the diagram a DSL wearing mermaid syntax. Worth doing
  deliberately, not by accident.
- **Task type.** `unverified → confirmed` is implementation; `→ completed` is
  research. E-2016 adds another status for research/brainstorm. One diagram,
  several lifecycles.

### Recommendation: GENERATE the diagram from the table (Mike, 2026-08-20)

Parsing was the wrong direction. Invert it: the Go transition table is the
source, and `docs/status-lifecycle.mmd` is a generated artifact. Drift stops
being something a test DETECTS and becomes something that cannot happen.

This is not a new mechanism — the repo already runs this pattern. `just
guide-index` regenerates a block in `docs/guide/index.md` between
`<!-- BEGIN generated: ... -->` / `<!-- END generated -->`, and `just
guide-check` exits non-zero on drift as a pre-land / CI gate. Apply the same
shape to the lifecycle.

What it collapses: today the `.mmd` is hand-authored, byte-copied into
README.md and docs/guide/index.md, and `tests/test_status_lifecycle_sync.py`
asserts the copies match. With generation the generator writes all of them, and
that test's job narrows to "is the committed artifact current" — the `gofmt -l`
shape.

It also fixes the two gaps above for free: `blocked` missing and `completed`
having no inbound edge are both artifacts of hand-maintenance.

And it makes the actor axis honest. Edge labels ("user approves", "session
claims") stop being a prose convention a reader has to trust and become RENDERED
from the table's actor column.

**Generate parts, not the whole file.** The editorial content — "Blocking is a
relation (blocked_by), not a state, so it is intentionally absent" — is a
hand-written preamble in the template. Only the states and edges are generated.
Same split `guide-index` already uses.

### One trap

**Deterministic order.** Go map iteration is randomized, so the table must be
ordered. Use `dtx.OrderedMap` from `github.com/mikeschinkel/go-dt/dtx` — already
in go-pkgs, already a dependency shape this repo uses. Order the output to READ
well — entry, happy path, reopening, terminal — not alphabetically.

(A second trap — "model the deliberate omission of `blocked` as a render flag" —
is withdrawn. There was no deliberate omission; see below.)

### `blocked` was never a decision, it was a contradiction

I had written that `blocked` is "intentionally absent" from the diagram. That
came from the diagram's own comment ("Blocking is a relation (blocked_by), not a
state, so it is intentionally absent") — an agent-written comment I repeated as
fact. Measured instead:

- `blocked` IS in the status vocabulary and in SQL status lists.
- 8 tasks currently hold `status=blocked`.
- `endless task block` creates a `blocked_by` RELATION and never touches status.
- Every sampled blocked-status task ALSO has the relation (E-634, E-721 → E-808;
  E-1515 → E-1479).

So the system ships both mechanisms, independently, and the comment asserts a
design the rest of the system contradicts. Worse, the duplication must go stale:
E-808 is `unverified`; when it reaches confirmed the relation stops blocking
automatically while `status=blocked` sits on E-634 and E-721 until a human edits
it.

Rather than encode the ambiguity as a flag, decide it: **ED-1572** proposes
blocking is a relation only, and `blocked` leaves the status vocabulary. If
accepted, the generator needs no render flag and the guard needs no special case.

### Sequencing

The table comes first, with the actor and type columns and the render flag. Then
the generator and its drift check, replacing the byte-sync test. Then the guard
consumes the same table. The two diagram gaps need no separate fix — they
disappear when the diagram is generated, provided `completed`'s inbound edges are
written into the table (they exist in the CLI today; they were only ever missing
from the picture).



---

## Where the guard hooks in (added 2026-08-25)

E-2067, spawned today, is the same shape as this task's guard half and lands
first: `endless task update --parent` can create a parent cycle because
`tasks.parent_id` has TWO writers and only one validates. `task move` emits
`task.moved`, whose executor walks the ancestor chain and refuses a circular
reference; `task update` emits `task.fields_updated`, whose executor carries
`parent_id` in its allowedFields map and writes it unchecked.

E-2067's fix is to lift that ancestor walk into a shared validator called from
both executors — mirroring `ValidateMaybeParentless`, which is already factored
that way and called from both. So by the time this task starts,
`execTaskFieldsUpdated` should have an established place to hang a
per-field validator, and one worked example of the pattern.

This task's transition-legality and actor-reality checks belong in exactly that
slot: `task update --status` reaches the same executor by the same route that
let the parent cycle through. Read E-2067's landed diff before designing the
hook — if it introduced a validator registry rather than a single call, follow
it rather than inventing a second arrangement.

Note the asymmetry that makes this more than a copy: the parent guard needs only
the tasks table, while transition legality needs the edge table this task's own
plan proposes. So the hook is shared; the data behind it is not.

## From the description

Two checks are missing and both were available from data Endless already had: (1) transition legality — `unplanned` to `unverified` is not an edge in docs/status-lifecycle.mmd; (2) actor reality — a session may not set work-progress statuses (`underway`, `unverified`) on a task it does not hold, and `unverified` should require that some session actually claimed it.

fields.title: Migrate the schema to goose versioned migrations
fields.description: Migrate the schema to goose: add the dependency, generate a baseline migration of the current schema, convert existing schema change files into embedded migrations, and baseline existing databases rather than replay them.
fields.analysis: -- the .go ones (which query the DB mid-migration, e.g. the sessions table rebuilds and the tmux binding backfill) become goose Go migrations, the .sql ones become goose SQL migrations. Count them at implementation time rather than trusting any number written here; the set grows. Embed the migration set into the binary so it ships with no file dependency. Existing populated databases must be BASELINED, not replayed: a real ledger already carries most of these changes, so the conversion has to mark them applied rather than re-run them. Note that _schema_version is a set of applied change-file basenames, not an ordered version, so baselining has to map that set onto goose's version sequence.

fields.title: Replace apply-on-connect with connect-time version checks
fields.description: Replace applying schema on every connect with a check that the database's migration version matches the binary's, with endless db upgrade as the explicit path that takes a backup first.
fields.analysis:
Also removes E-1818's schema-passive mode, which becomes unnecessary once no connect applies schema: the mode exists to stop a binary mutating a DB it merely opened, and nothing needs suppressing when nothing applies.

## The real ledger and schema version 1

E-2019 landed and the ledger is recorded at goose version 1. Measured then, the ledger did NOT match what version 1 declares: a pre-rename `tasks.status` default of 'needs_plan', a `tasks_updated_at` trigger missing its no-op-write guard, an unused `tasks.focus_id`, 11 tables left by removed features (two of them from change files recorded as applied whose DROPs never took effect), and 5 orphaned rows.

That was cleaned up by hand on 2026-09-17, deliberately with no task (Mike's call: data cleansing needs no record). Backups taken before each step are in ~/.config/endless/backups/. Measured after, against a database freshly built from schema.sql:

- Objects: identical set. Nothing extra, nothing missing.
- Columns, types, defaults and foreign keys: identical on every table.
- `PRAGMA foreign_key_check`: 0 violations. `integrity_check`: ok.
- Still different, both cosmetic: column ORDER on tasks, decisions, task_landings and errors (ALTER-appended rather than declared order), and `session_statuses_session_recent_idx` spelled `(session_id asc, created_at desc)` rather than `(session_id, created_at DESC)` — the same index.

Consequence for this task: if the direction rules ever want more than the recorded version integer, a SEMANTIC shape comparison (object set, pragma_table_info columns/types/defaults, pragma_foreign_key_list) now passes on the real ledger. An exact comparison of sqlite_master text still does not, and never will without rebuilding four tables to reorder columns — so do not build one.

## What E-2019 leaves for this task to build on

- schema.Migrate(db) is the single way a database acquires its schema (monitor.DB, the sandbox seeder, the ledger projector, tests, and Python via `endless-go event migrate`).
- schema.DBVersion(ctx, db) reads the version a database is recorded at; schema.LatestVersion() reads the highest version the BINARY carries. The direction rules are a comparison of those two.
- schema.Seed(db) applies the enum mirrors and is called on every Migrate. It is deliberately NOT a migration: it preserves E-1659's self-heal. When this task stops applying schema on connect, decide explicitly whether Seed keeps running — the enum gates in monitor.DB() depend on it.
- Migrate also turns on foreign key enforcement for the connection, because schema.sql's leading PRAGMA used to do that as a side effect of being exec'd. Keep that property if Migrate stops being called on connect: something else has to own it.
- 00001_baseline.sql is the only migration allowed to be idempotent (every statement carries IF NOT EXISTS). A later migration must not copy that.

## From the description

DB behind an installed binary auto-applies forward; DB behind a candidate binary refuses, since a candidate may never migrate the real ledger; DB ahead of any binary halts. endless db upgrade is the explicit path, taking a backup first so a bad release rolls back by restore (E-1942). Three things fold in. (1) Refusal is per-surface: the Claude hook fires on every event, so erroring loudly turns one mismatch into machine-wide noise -- follow E-1962's silent no-op plus a recorded fault, while interactive surfaces refuse loudly.

(2) The land window, assigned here by E-1972: the seconds where the DB is migrated and the installed binary is not, which last time printed fifty near-identical errors after a SUCCESSFUL land. (3) db.py's _incomplete_schema_hint points at a change file -- deferred to E-2158, which deletes its subject.

fields.title: Generate schema.sql from the goose migrations
fields.description: Generate schema.sql from the goose migration set as a readable documentation snapshot, with a check that fails when the committed copy is stale.
fields.context: schema.sql stops being applied but remains valuable as a readable snapshot of the full schema for someone studying it.
fields.analysis:
## What E-2019 leaves this task to generate from

The migration set is internal/schema/migrations/, embedded via //go:embed and driven by goose as a library. 00001_baseline.sql was produced by dumping sqlite_master, in creation order, from a database built by schema.sql, then mechanically re-injecting IF NOT EXISTS (SQLite does not store that clause, and the baseline must stay idempotent so the real ledger reaches version 1 by an inert replay). The generator used is a throwaway; this task writes the durable one, in the other direction.

Three things a naive generator would get wrong:

1. FTS5 shadow tables. schema.sql declares one virtual table, session_messages_fts. SQLite then creates session_messages_fts_data/_idx/_docsize/_config, and those appear in sqlite_master like any other table. Declaring them is wrong — the fts5 module owns them. Detect with `SELECT name FROM pragma_table_list WHERE type='shadow'` (SQLite 3.37+), not by name pattern.
2. The enum seeds are NOT in the migration set. They live in internal/schema/seeds.sql and are applied by schema.Seed() after every migration run, so E-1659's self-heal survives. A generated schema.sql that omits them describes a database that fails every integrity gate on first connect; a generated one that includes them has to say where they actually come from.
3. The three leading PRAGMAs (journal_mode, busy_timeout, foreign_keys) are not in the migration set either — they configure a connection, and journal_mode cannot change inside goose's transaction. Every opener sets them itself.

## The cost this task should weigh explicitly

schema.sql is 1,323 lines, and a large fraction of it is commentary that exists nowhere else — the E-1960 index-naming trap, the E-1929 view-vs-index ordering constraint, the ID-append rule on session_task_relations, the reasoning behind the write-once trigger. A generator that emits DDL produces a file that is accurate and says none of that. The description's fallback ("delete schema.sql rather than keep a hand-maintained copy") would delete the commentary with it. Consider a third option: move the prose into the migrations that own each object, so generation has something to carry forward.

While both files exist, internal/schema/migrate_test.go's TestMigrate_MatchesSchemaSQL pins them equal in both directions — a schema.sql edited without a migration fails, and a migration added without mirroring into schema.sql fails. That test is what this task replaces with real generation.

## sqlc, if it is still on the roadmap

Checked 2026-09-16. sqlc reads a goose migration directory natively (schema: <migrations dir>, engine: "sqlite"; sqlc names atlas, dbmate, golang-migrate, goose, sql-migrate and tern) and ignores Down sections. Two constraints worth keeping in mind here, because they shape what the migration set may contain:

- sqlc parses migration files in LEXICOGRAPHIC order, which diverges from goose's numeric order unless filenames are zero-padded. 00001_baseline.sql already is; keep the padding.
- sqlc can only read SQL migrations. A goose GO migration is invisible to it, so any DDL expressed in Go silently disappears from the schema sqlc models. Keep DDL in .sql migrations and put data work in a separate step.
- sqlc gained virtual-table/FTS5 support in 1.31.0 with known rough edges (the fts5 token is case-sensitive — this schema spells it lowercase, which is the working case — and the implicit rowid is not modeled). session_messages_fts is the one object most likely to need attention if sqlc is adopted.

## From the description

If generation proves impractical, the fallback is deleting schema.sql rather than keeping a hand-maintained copy -- a stale snapshot presented as the schema is worse than none.

fields.title: Decide the upgrade policy and schema compatibility range
fields.description: Decide whether a normal user's binary refuses or auto-upgrades on a schema mismatch after upgrading, and whether the connect check admits a declared compatibility range instead of an exact version match.
fields.context: ED-1567 settled that ordinary connects verify and refuse, confirmed for self_dev.
fields.analysis:
Renaming note: this task was filed as 'decide the non-self_dev upgrade policy and whether expand-contract becomes a rule'. The expand-contract half was settled as ED-1568 (hard rule) before this task was started, leaving the compatibility-range consequence in its place. A policy differing between self_dev and non-self_dev is defensible since the modes genuinely differ, but it means the dangerous path gets the least real-world exercise -- worth weighing against the extra step a refusal costs every user after every upgrade.

## From the description

(1) A normal user has one installed binary, so the two-binary problem does not arise; on a mismatch after upgrading endless, does that binary refuse (uniform behavior, one tested path, an extra step after every upgrade) or auto-upgrade forward (no interruption, but preserves the 'any binary may migrate whatever DB it opens' property this decision exists to remove)? (2) ED-1568 made expand-contract a rule, and it only pays off if the connect check admits a compatibility RANGE rather than an exact match -- goose gives a linear version, so two schema-compatible binaries compare unequal and refuse anyway.

Binaries need to declare the range they support.

How harsh the refusal must be depends on how often a mismatch can happen at all, which is what the range determines.

fields.title: Enforce the own-task-only rule at the verify runner
fields.description: Enforce in the verify runner itself that a task's verify script runs only in that task's own worktree, refusing it anywhere else instead of relying on prose.
fields.context:
CLAUDE.md says a tests/tasks/e-NNNN-verify.sh is valid only immediately before land, in the worktree for its own task, and that you must not run another task's script.

this session ran e-1956-verify.sh from E-1185's worktree and reported the violation as "not required". Nothing refused it.
fields.analysis:
## Why prose is not enough

The rule already exists and is unambiguous. It was read, understood, paraphrased into "not required", and broken — by a session that could quote it. An agent's compliance with prose is negotiable at the moment it is inconvenient, which is precisely the moment enforcement has to exist.

## The load-bearing fix: guard inside the script

Each script already resolves its worktree root via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` in `main()`. Add a guard there: ask endless which task this worktree holds and exit 2 unless it matches the script's own id, with a refusal that names the sanctioned runners (`endless verify <id>`, `just verify <id>`) rather than just saying no.

Put it in a shared helper the scripts source, not copied into each — there are ~40 scripts and a copied guard is ~40 chances to omit it. Add it to whatever template new scripts are written from so one authored next month inherits it. Both sanctioned runners already know the task id, so they pass by construction.

This layer works for every user, every harness, and a human at a shell prompt.

## Second symptom, same root cause

A landed script's source-shape greps go stale on legitimate refactors of code the script does not own. `e-1956-verify.sh` lines 155 and 161 grep for literal spellings — `!isTerminal(r.Status)` and a JOIN clause — that E-1185 has since factored away. The properties they stood for are intact and now pinned by behavioral tests on both sides (`TestReplacedByNote_TerminalGate`, `test_replaced_by_map_ignores_a_removed_replacement`, and their duplicates counterparts).

Under prose-only rules that stale grep is a landmine: the next refactorer runs it, sees red, and "fixes" working code to match — which is exactly what happened here. Under the guard it is inert, because nobody outside E-1956's worktree can reach it. One cause, two symptoms, one task.

## Optional second layer, not a substitute

A PreToolUse hook refusing a mismatched verify-script invocation, mirroring E-1226's hook for `sqlite3 .endless` paths. It refuses earlier and can teach at the point of the mistake. But it is harness-specific per E-1962 and does not cover a human at a shell, so it cannot carry the rule alone.

## PRODUCT note

Nothing here is Endless-specific. Any project using Endless accumulates per-task verify scripts with the same property: they are gates for one task at one moment, they look like a regression suite, and they rot. The guard belongs in the shipped scaffolding, not in this repo's scripts only. `self_dev` changes nothing — the worktree-to-task lookup is the same call in both modes.

# Addendum — a bulk sweep, and why hermeticism is not an available fix (E-2071, 2026-08-26)

## What happened

Escalation from the single wrong script this task was filed on: a session ran
EVERY script — `for f in tests/tasks/*.sh` — 197 of them, as a "project-wide
regression check" before handing off. The rationalization was not "the rule does
not apply"; it was that running the suite is what you do before you hand work
over, and these live under `tests/`.

`e-1202-verify.sh` drives the real hook binary with a synthetic payload carrying
`session_id: "e1202-verify"`. The hook did what it always does: wrote a sessions
row into the MAIN database and bound it to the caller's live tmux pane. Two
session identities then claimed one pane, and `_resolve_companion` refuses an
ambiguous sibling set — so `esu` and every companion-resolving command stopped
working in Mike's shell for the rest of the session. The row is still there;
ending it needs a hand-driven SessionEnd.

## The finding that changes the mitigation set

`cmd/endless-go/main.go` PinMainDB's the `hook` and `tmux` subcommands
UNCONDITIONALLY — an explicit `--config-dir` is honored, but hook traffic is
otherwise pinned to main regardless of cwd or XDG_CONFIG_HOME, by design
(E-1450/E-1429: a fired hook is real-world activity in the real database).

So for any verify script that exercises hook behavior, "make it hermetic" is not
on the table in the usual way. The newer scripts' isolation pattern — a throwaway
config dir under the cache sandbox root, CLI run from outside the repo — does not
contain a hook invocation unless the script also threads `--config-dir` into it,
which the older ones do not and which is easy to omit silently.

This strengthens the case that the REFUSAL is the load-bearing defense, not
containment. A script that cannot run outside its own worktree cannot pollute
anything, whatever it does internally.

## Location, as a complement

The guard is the fix. But `tests/tasks/` is what makes the mistake reachable:
the scripts are shelved beside a real suite, `just test` runs `tests/`, and any
glob over `tests/` sweeps them in. Whatever the guard's final shape, consider
whether these belong under a path that does not read as a suite — cheap, and it
removes the invitation rather than only refusing it. (Filed separately as E-2077,
declined as a duplicate of this task; recorded here so the option is not lost.)

## The asymmetry that makes this agent-shaped

Recovering from the damage above surfaced the sharpest version of the problem.
`internal/hookcmd/claude.go` opens `runClaude` with `if !supportedAgent() {
return nil }` — silent, nil, no stdout, exit 0. The predicate reads the PROCESS
environment (`CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=cli`).

So the same script, byte for byte:

- Run by a human at a prompt: the hook gate closes, nothing happens, rc=0. Inert.
- Run by an agent's shell tool: the process IS Claude Code, every harness gate
  opens, and the writes land in the main database.

Mike could not even undo the damage by hand — the recovery command was silently
inert for him and worked immediately from the agent's shell.

This is not incidental. The scripts are dangerous SPECIFICALLY in the hands of
the actor most likely to run them wrongly, and harmless in the hands of the one
who would notice. Any guard designed against a human operator is testing the
case that was never a problem. The refusal has to fire in the agent's process,
which argues for the shared-helper guard in the scripts themselves (which runs
whoever invokes it) over anything keyed on who is asking.

## From the description

That is prose, and prose is advisory to an agent that can rationalize it:

fields.title: Queue judgment-shaped status transitions for an async judge
fields.description: Queue task update's judgment-shaped status transitions, such as a material description edit, for an async judge that holds both versions, instead of deciding them inline by byte comparison.
fields.context: task update decides four status transitions inline, and the two judgment-shaped ones do not actually judge: 'material description edit' is implemented as byte inequality against the old value. --keep-status is the manual patch for that gap, which is why it draws an inline decision on every edit.

fields.title: Restart agents and jobs onto the new binary after upgrade
fields.description: Restart long-running processes still on a superseded binary, such as background agents and the jobs runner, onto the new one as part of a schema upgrade, instead of letting each halt mid-flight.
fields.notes: E-1704 is the surface that decides which binary a process should be running; it moves that choice into the binary itself via self-re-exec, governed by E-1972's verified-compatible policy.
fields.context:
ED-1570 halts a binary whose schema version is behind the database.

After an upgrade migrates the ledger, every long-running process still holding the old binary image — background agents, the jobs runner — halts on its next connect and dies mid-flight, which can take down tens of live sessions at once.
fields.analysis: Halting is correct and must not be relaxed,

fields.title: Give planners a role preface and refuse file:line references
fields.description: Give the planning agent a role preface saying its job is invariants, not details an implementor would find, and add a check that refuses file:line references in durable task content.
fields.context: Plans keep arriving micro-managed: file line numbers, symbol inventories, path-by-path maps. They are stale before pickup and they invite the implementor to follow the map instead of looking.

fields.title: Record agent task reads as referenced
fields.description: Record the tasks an agent reads with task show or task detail against the current session under the 'referenced' relation, as machine-local state that never reaches the committed ledger.
fields.notes: Deferred half of E-1696, which landed the vocabulary, the precedence ladder, the session task verbs and the display tier.
fields.analysis:
# Why this is separate from E-1696, and why it IS blocked

Split from E-1696 with Mike on 2026-08-21. E-1696 landed everything that needed
no new storage: the `referenced` + `queued` vocabulary, the upgrade-only
precedence ladder replacing E-1462's set-once rule, `session task add`/`remove`,
and the relation display tier. This is the auto-capture gate itself.

## Prerequisite status

- **Actor detection — SATISFIED.** E-1462's analysis named agent-vs-human
  detection as a prerequisite; E-1962/E-1966 landed `agent_env.present()` /
  `internal/agentenv`. The gate keys on it directly.
- **Machine-user ledger — E-1673.** A hard `blocked_by`. See below.

## The volume argument (measured 2026-08-21)

The committed ledger holds 8,027 events. The entire "muddy bucket" —
`session_status.*`, `focus.*`, `session_tasks.ordered`: committed but never
replayed — is 22 lines, 0.27%.

Read capture changes that. `task show` is step 1 of `endless guide`'s happy
path, and the session implementing E-1696 made nine `task show` calls before
writing a line of code. Against ~128 recorded `task.claimed` events that is
1000+ events — the 4th-largest kind in the ledger, larger than `task.landed`
(576) — growing without bound, every line saying "this developer glanced at
E-1234". 458 of the last 899 commits already touch the ledger.

Per Mike (2026-06-30, folded into E-1462's Extension): reads are session-local,
ephemeral and per-developer, so they go to a gitignored machine-user ledger, not
the shared one.

## Why blocked_by E-1673, and not the narrow workaround

This task was FIRST filed carrying its own narrow `local/` routing for its one
event kind, related to E-1673 rather than blocked by it, so it could land
without waiting. Mike corrected that on 2026-08-21 and the narrow routing is
removed. Recording why, because the reasoning generalizes:

Duplicating a blocker's small load-bearing piece into the blocked task is a real
technique — it is what unblocked E-1696, which needed nothing from E-1673 at all
and would otherwise have been parked behind an unapproved 8-workstream epic. But
it is a COST paid to buy a benefit, and the benefit is "this ships sooner". Here
there was no such need: nothing downstream is waiting on this task. Paying the
cost anyway was pure loss.

The cost was not hypothetical. E-1673's design explicitly forbids the shape the
workaround would have introduced:

> Scope must be declared, never defaulted. [...] Do not let "project is the root
> default" decay into "undeclared is fine."

A one-kind opt-in is a convention where E-1673 wants a gate — so the "narrow
subset E-1673 later subsumes" framing was too generous. It would have left a
half-gate for E-1673 to unpick, plus a second round of `.gitignore` and
`endless register` scaffolding.

**The unlock is E-1673's own approval, not a workaround.** E-1673 is `submitted`
with a plan marked "Design is locked; this plan is option-free", carries no
`blocked_by` of its own, and its parent epic E-1671 is a parent, not a gate. It
can be approved and landed on its own schedule. That makes `blocked_by` here
honest AND cheap: the blocker actually moves.

## Scope

1. Emit a new event kind for the read capture from the `task show` /
   `task detail` read path, gated on `agent_env.present()` and on a resolvable
   session. Declared `machine-user` scope, so E-1673's emit gate routes it to
   `.endless/db-ledger/local/` — this task adds a declaration, not a routing
   mechanism.
2. No new executor logic needed: `upsertSessionTask` already accepts
   `RelationReferenced`, and the ladder already handles read-before-claim
   (pinned by `TestSessionTasks_RelationUpgrades` — the referenced→goal case).
3. Revisit collapsing the referenced tier behind a flag once real volume exists.
   E-1696 shipped dimming plus a hard sink, which E-1462's Extension offers as
   the alternative to collapsing; whether a `… N referenced` footer is also
   wanted is a question only real read volume can answer.

## From the description

Read capture is high-volume machine-user state that must never reach the committed ledger, so this declares its event kind machine-user scope and relies on E-1673's emit-time routing gate rather than carrying any routing of its own.

fields.title: Show a session whom to message when it affects another
fields.description: Show a session whom to message, with the reply affordance inline, at the moment one of its actions is recognized as affecting another live session's work, instead of a standing roster.
fields.context:
A session cannot act on information it never considers.

Today the who-to-talk-to data is available on request, which requires knowing the command exists AND thinking to run it at the right moment; the second half is where it fails.
fields.analysis:
TRIGGERS. All detectable from data Endless already holds -- joins over session_tasks, tasks.status = 'underway', and sessions.state. No new capture required.

1. An inbound message arrives. Carry the reply affordance with it, not merely the content.
2. You link a task held by a live underway session (block, relate, cleans-up, replace).
3. You record a decision that governs such a task.
4. You edit, re-status or file a task a live session is holding.

EVIDENCE, from session ES-1105 on E-1944 (2026-08-21). Every one of these fired during a single brainstorm and none produced a notification.

(1) Another session sent findings from E-2010. They were folded in and one claim corrected. Replying never entered consideration -- not a judgment made and lost.
(2) E-2020 was blocked by E-1704, and E-1704 by E-1972, minutes before E-1972 was spawned into a live session.
(3) ED-1570 supplies exactly the 'verified compatible' test E-1972 was missing, and neither side was told.

DESIGN NOTE. The unit is the affected work, not the session roster: 'what you just did affects ES-NNNN, reach them with X'. A roster answers a question the session is not asking at the moment it is shown.


## The trigger list is entirely OUTBOUND (noted 2026-09-11)

All four triggers above are things YOU did to work someone else holds. The
mirror image is missing: something happened to work YOU hold or surfaced, and
nobody told you. A task you surfaced being claimed is the plain example — the
surfacing session gets `status: submitted → underway` from the field trigger and
no session id, so it learns that someone picked the task up but not who, and
cannot tell a spawn from a claim in place.

Worth folding in whenever this is planned, because the affordance differs by
direction: outbound is "what you just did affects ES-NNNN, reach them with X",
inbound is "ES-NNNN is now working E-NNNN, which you surfaced". Only the
outbound half needs E-1936 to have chosen a transport.

NOT a reason to prioritise this task. An earlier version of this note argued
that the missing inbound notice was why handoffs told Mike to spawn tasks he had
already spawned. That diagnosis was wrong: `endless task show <id> --llm`
already prints `touched_by=claimed ES-NNNN (E-NNNN) [working]`, so the data is
present in the exact command the handoff path is told to run. The defect was in
the handoff rules, not in what Endless reports, and it is fixed there. This task
remains what its title says — who to message — and is deferrable.

## From the description

A standing roster in additionalContext is the wrong fix -- it bloats context and earns notice-blindness, and one session can spawn ten tasks.

Transport-agnostic: this decides WHEN a session is told whom to reach, while E-1936 decides the transport it reaches them with.

fields.title: Remove the channel command and endless-channel MCP server
fields.description: Remove the dead channel surface: the CLI command and all its subcommands, the endless-channel MCP server, and the associated tables and Go and Python code paths.
fields.notes: Independent of E-1936, which designs the replacement -- retiring the dead surface does not wait on deciding what succeeds it, and neither blocks the other.
fields.context: The channel surface is dead: the commands no longer work, and the channels table is keyed on the same non-unique sessions.process string behind E-1898's incident, making it the last consumer of that old key.
fields.analysis: Check for verify suites and guide sections that reference channels, and for tasks parked against the old surface (E-1489 port channel DB access to Go, E-1522 cover channelcmd MCP server via mcp-go test client, E-840 simplify channel connect) which become obsolete on removal.

fields.title: Stop guiding report-gate-off projects to the reply minimizer
fields.description: Stop the guide telling sessions to use task report on projects whose report gate is off, and add a runtime check that the deployed minimizer prompt keeps commands the user must run.
fields.context: A session on a gate-off project is therefore told to use a channel that will not gate it, which its own code comment forbids.

fields.title: Fix the orchestration-guide verify suite's stale checks
fields.description: Fix the four failing checks in the orchestration-guide verify suite that pin since-rewritten guide prose, deciding per check whether the guide or the assertion is wrong.
fields.context:
tests/tasks/e-1573-verify.sh fails 4 of 42 checks on main, unrelated to E-2029 (verified identical on main and in the E-2029 worktree).

One root cause: the suite pins exact prose from docs/guide/orchestration.md, and that prose has been rewritten since without the suite being updated.

The four: (1) 'unknown type falls back to the `task` variant' — sentence reworded; (2) 'All `needs_plan`' and (3) 'All `in_progress`' — assert the pre-rename status vocabulary, now unplanned/underway; (4) 'spawn section is id-free (shipped-doc rule)' — E-1851, E-1953 and E-698 have since been written into the shipped guide, which the rule forbids.
fields.analysis: Fix is to decide per check whether the guide or the assertion is wrong: (4) is likely a real guide defect (strip the ids), (2)/(3) are stale assertions, (1) needs a read.

fields.title: Add a user-level template override directory
fields.description: Add a user-level template layer between the project templates and the embedded defaults, so one override applies across all of a user's projects.
fields.context:
templatecmd resolves a template as <project_root>/.endless/templates/<name>.local.tmpl, then <name>.tmpl, then the Go embed.

That is per-project only: a user who wants the same handoff or guide wording across every project they work on must copy the override into each one, and re-copy it whenever a project is added.

Surfaced from E-2030, where gating the guide on report_gate raised the question of where a user edits shipped text.

fields.title: Restore verify scripts that drive the hook from a bare shell
fields.description: Restore verify scripts that pipe into the hook from a bare shell so they exercise it again, since the hook became a silent no-op on unrecognized harnesses and they now pass without testing anything.
fields.context:
E-1962 made `hook claude` a silent no-op on an unrecognized agent harness, and a bare shell is one.

Confirmed in tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh.

fields.title: Replace apply-on-connect with versioned migrations
fields.description: Replace applying schema on every connect with versioned migrations: adopt goose as the source of schema, generate schema.sql as documentation, and require binary and database versions to agree.
fields.notes: Children were filed as free-floating siblings held together only by cleans_up E-1944; this gives them a home.
fields.context: Umbrella for the schema-governance work E-1944 decided (ED-1566/1567/1570) after the 2026-08-10 outage, in which a candidate binary wrote a column the real ledger lacked and session tracking went down for 30 minutes.

fields.description: Stop commands run with --db sandbox writing non-database files, such as decision mirrors, into the real project root and committing them, by making the database target govern every file write.
fields.context:
`--db sandbox` isolates the DB and, since E-1729, the event ledger — but nothing else.

Hit on E-1920: a sandbox-routed `decision add` wrote decision mirrors into the worktree and auto-committed two junk commits onto the task branch.

E-1729 already fixed this exact mechanism for the ledger and established the shape (sandbox-local dir under ConfigDir, no git commit, since a sandbox is disposable and not a repo), but it was applied at one call site instead of made a rule, so E-1747's doc mirrors re-broke it.

fields.description: Stop reporting a query that fails on a missing table or column as an uninitialized database, and name the missing column and the schema change to apply instead.
fields.context: Hit on E-1920: `decision show` selected a column added by an unapplied schema change, and the message claimed the whole DB was uninitialized while `decision list` (not selecting that column) worked fine in the same second.
fields.analysis: The handler should distinguish a missing-table or missing-column error from a genuinely unschema'd file, and name the column and the change file to apply.

fields.description: Stop using 'ledger' for the SQLite database, which is a rebuildable projection of the durable ledger, across live code, docs, templates and user-facing refusal text.
fields.context: 31 sites in live code, docs and templates;
fields.analysis:
# "Ledger" already means something else

The db-ledger (`.endless/db-ledger/*.jsonl`) is the permanent record of task
state; the SQLite database is a rebuildable projection of it. CLAUDE.md says so
in its own words. Using "ledger" for the database collapses the distinction that
architecture rests on, and it does it in the two places most likely to mislead:
agent-facing comments, and the user-facing `--db` refusal.

## Scope

31 sites in live code, docs and templates. Two are user-facing:

    src/endless/config.py   "  --db main     the real ledger — managing the project"
    src/endless/cli.py      "--db main (the real ledger) or --db sandbox (this worktree's test DB). "

The rest are comments, docstrings and two guide pages. `internal/monitor/db.go`
carries the most, and is where the term does the most damage — it is the file
that decides which database a process opens.

## Explicitly OUT of scope: `tests/tasks/*-verify.sh`

There are 80 more occurrences there. Leave every one of them.

A verify script is a pre-land gate, valid only immediately before its own land,
in its own worktree. A landed one is spent — nothing should ever run it again —
so its wording cannot mislead anyone and editing it is churn against an artifact
with no future. E-1975 already filed and declined a task (E-2033) that misread
this rule; do not re-derive it.

## Wording

`--db main` and `--db sandbox` already establish the vocabulary. Say "the main
database" and "the sandbox database" (or "this worktree's sandbox"). Avoid "real
ledger", "the real DB" and "the ledger" wherever the SQLite database is meant.

The user-facing strings deserve Mike's eye rather than a mechanical
substitution: the refusal text is the first thing an agent hits when it gets the
flag wrong, and it is currently the clearest statement in the product of what
the two databases are for.

## From the description

the 80 in tests/tasks/*-verify.sh are deliberately out of scope, being spent pre-land gates.

fields.title: Make an appeal able to restore an over-cut draft
fields.description: Make an appeal of a minimizer cut able to restore what the appealed pass removed, instead of re-minimizing the draft and possibly returning even less.
fields.context:
report_cmd runs the appeal through the SAME minimize prompt with no separate prompt and no relationship to the pass it appeals, so it is simply another independent minimization whose input happens to contain an argument — free to return LESS than what it is appealing.

Observed twice in one session on E-1920: the first pass dropped the answers to two directly-asked questions, and the appeal dropped those plus the appeal argument itself, leaving disconnected fragments; the agent then had no recourse left because the budget is one.
fields.analysis:
No prompt wording can fix this, which is why it is a task rather than a denylist override — monotonicity is a mechanical property, like the invariant vetoes.

Options: require the appeal's output to cover the spans it argues for, or present both passes and let the user pick.

fields.title: Add report log and report show for reading past drafts
fields.description: Add report log to list recent reply drafts and report show to display one draft with its raw and minimized text side by side.
fields.notes: Design already settled in E-1959; see the link.
fields.context: There is no way to read a past draft. `task report --raw` prints only the newest one, so once a reply is minimized the user cannot see what was cut, and cannot judge or label it.

fields.title: Honor a hand-edited minimize instruction
fields.description: Honor the minimize instruction written in the report prompts override file when task report shortens replies, instead of always reading the promoted instruction from the database.
fields.context: So a hand-written instruction has had no effect since the first time the background job promoted one, and nothing says so — while denylist, judge and generate overrides in the same file still work. report_prompts.py's own docstring promises the opposite.

fields.description: Make the reply minimizer safe to leave enabled by adding a way to read what it cut, a working recourse when it cuts wrongly, and a self-tuning loop that actually runs.
fields.notes: Disabled in this project until the pieces that make it safe to leave on exist.
fields.context: The reply minimizer ships enabled but has never been calibrated: no way to read what it cut, no working recourse when it cuts wrongly, and a self-tuning loop that has never run.

fields.title: Add an observe-only minimizer mode
fields.description: Add an observe-only minimizer mode between on and off that still records drafts and turn context through task report but cuts and enforces nothing, letting the agent send its own reply.
fields.context: Turning the minimizer off also stops drafts being recorded, so the corpus stops growing during exactly the period it would be most useful to accumulate one.
fields.analysis: That keeps a replayable corpus building while the channel is untrusted, so when it is switched back on there is real material to calibrate against instead of starting from zero.
